title: The Trump DOJ Quietly Intervened to Ink a Huge Payout to a Trump Golf Pro
author: Alex Mierjeski
content:
Top Trump administration officials intervened to help a longtime golf pro at
Trump National Golf Club Hudson Valley secure a half-million-dollar payout
from the IRS. A company connected to Trump’s media business also got a half-
million.

The deal grew out of a little-noticed federal class-action lawsuit filed in
2025 by five individuals and companies. The group got $2.5 million after
accusing the IRS of failing to protect their tax information.

[The law permits a $1,000
payment](https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/26/7431) to victims for each
instance of an unauthorized inspection or disclosure of tax data. In this
case, however, the government’s monetary settlement is 250 times higher than
what the law calls for given the allegations. Victims can receive more money
if they show actual damages, but multiple officials say such cases almost
never result in payments approaching this size. These generous settlements
have raised concerns because IRS Office of Chief Counsel attorneys were not
consulted about the settlement terms, as is standard practice, according to
people familiar with the case and documents seen by ProPublica.

What’s more, those payouts didn’t resolve the lawsuit. After the settlement
was made, two more people came forward seeking to [continue the
litigation](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28922607-notice-to-add-
plaintiffs-safe-harbor-class-action/) — and both are connected to Trump
businesses. One is a retired accountant who worked at the same Trump property
as the golf pro. The second appears to be a former lifeguard at a different
Trump golf club in Westchester County, New York.

Gil Rothenberg, a law professor at American University who ran the appellate
section at the Justice Department tax division for 15 years before leaving in
2019, said the deal “is not passing the smell test.”

“It’s not just the amount that I find odd and unusual,” he told ProPublica.
“It’s the fact that this settlement amount occurred before any final decision
by the district court, and basically the DOJ is giving up any right to
appeal.”

The [case in
question](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28922518-consolidated-class-
action-complaint-safe-harbor/) is Safe Harbor International LLC v. Booz Allen
Hamilton, Internal Revenue Service and the U.S. Department of the Treasury,
brought in Maryland federal court. Plaintiffs claim that the IRS and the
government contractor Booz Allen failed to implement proper safeguards and
were negligent in allowing Booz Allen employee Charles Littlejohn to steal tax
records and give them to news organizations, including ProPublica.

[President Donald Trump sued over similar
claims](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.flsd.706172/gov.uscourts.flsd.706172.1.0_4.pdf)
earlier this year, seeking $10 billion in damages. In response, then-acting
Attorney General Todd Blanche [announced a $1.776 billion “anti-weaponization
fund”](https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/justice-department-announces-anti-
weaponization-fund) to resolve the case. That settlement was structured to
grant the president’s inner circle the authority to green-light payouts of
government money to whomever they wanted. The public erupted in outrage.
Democratic and even a small number of Republican lawmakers objected to the
proposed fund, and the department dropped the idea as Blanche sought Senate
confirmation for his position.

Critics fear that the DOJ’s unusual payment in the Safe Harbor __ case could
be a backdoor way to revive something similar to the controversial slush fund.
In all, [plaintiffs claim the size of the
class](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28922518-consolidated-class-
action-complaint-safe-harbor/?mode=document#document/p19/a2836217) is “in the
tens or hundreds of thousands.” If a significant number of those plaintiffs
secured the same payment, the total liability for the federal government could
reach into the billions of dollars. A judge has yet to rule on whether to
allow the case to proceed.

That group could include other Trump allies and friends. It even “opens the
door to Trump himself benefiting from this settlement,” said John Koskinen,
who served as IRS commissioner from 2013 to 2017.

Spokespeople for the Justice Department and IRS said they would not comment on
a pending case. A White House spokesperson said that the Justice Department is
“promoting efficient resolution of cases to avoid extraordinary liability.”

Between 2018 and 2020, Littlejohn, the Booz Allen contractor, leaked
confidential IRS data to ProPublica and The New York Times, he has said. The
data included years of Trump’s taxes and information on thousands of the
wealthiest people in the country.

* * *

### Do You Have a Justice Department Tip for ProPublica?

If you know about this case and the government’s handling of it, please
contact our reporting team. I’m grateful for any documents that sources can
share. Protecting sources is something I take very seriously.

**Avi Asher-Schapiro**

If you have tips about Big Tech and the Trump administration, please get in
touch.

[Contact Me](https://www.propublica.org/people/avi-asher-schapiro)

* * *

ProPublica [published stories](https://www.propublica.org/article/the-secret-
irs-files-trove-of-never-before-seen-records-reveal-how-the-wealthiest-avoid-
income-tax) on the tax-avoidance strategies of the ultrawealthy. [The New York
Times reported](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2020/09/27/us/donald-
trump-taxes.html) in 2020 on how Trump declared large annual losses to avoid
paying taxes. Together, the two news organizations reported that Trump was
fighting with the IRS over a long-running audit that could have [cost him $100
million](https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-irs-audit-chicago-hotel-
taxes).

[Littlejohn pleaded guilty](https://www.justice.gov/archives/opa/pr/irs-
contractor-pleads-guilty-disclosing-tax-return-information-news-organizations)
in October 2023 to unauthorized disclosure of tax information. A judge
[sentenced him to five years in
prison](https://www.justice.gov/criminal/criminal-vns/case/united-states-v-
charles-littlejohn).

The IRS sent letters to more than [400,000 individuals and
businesses](https://judiciary.house.gov/sites/evo-subsites/republicans-
judiciary.house.gov/files/evo-media-
document/Jordan%20%20%28Data%20Breach%20and%20Security%29%20-%20Final.pdf) to
alert them that their taxpayer information had been “inappropriately
disclosed” by Littlejohn. As ProPublica has previously stated, we obtained the
tax return information of the top 0.001% of individuals by income, a figure in
the thousands. Limited information about other entities appears in the records
only to the extent that it is related to the group of top earners.

A number of taxpayers who received the notice filed civil lawsuits demanding
compensation from the IRS and Booz Allen.

The Safe Harbor __ class-action initially brought together five such
plaintiffs who, at first glance, had nothing in common apart from having
received an IRS notice about the leak.

Safe Harbor International is an obscure LLC incorporated in Delaware. It has
no website or public presence and was most recently registered to a
residential home in Washington, D.C. When ProPublica knocked on the door, the
person living there said they’d never heard of the company.

Safe Harbor’s investors include [Donald
Wilson](http://linkedin.com/in/donwilsonjr), who leads a Chicago-based
financial trading firm. Last March, the [Securities and Exchange Commission
dropped a case](https://www.sec.gov/enforcement-litigation/litigation-
releases/lr-26276) brought during the Biden administration against a crypto
company that Wilson controlled. A few months later, Wilson’s firm said it had
[invested $100
million](https://www.ft.com/content/548161ee-0cfb-4f0c-90ea-b3ff3567f09d?syn-25a6b1a6=1)
in the president’s publicly traded media company, Trump Media and Technology
Group, the owner of Truth Social.

A spokesperson for Wilson said he is a passive shareholder in Safe Harbor and
“was unaware of this lawsuit until last week and has had no involvement in the
litigation or any settlement discussions.” The spokesperson added that there
was no connection between Wilson’s Trump Media investment and the SEC’s
dismissal. “There was no quid pro quo, and the investment was not made in
exchange for any regulatory action,” the spokesperson said.

The other four plaintiffs who ultimately joined [Safe Harbor’s
suit](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28922518-consolidated-class-
action-complaint-safe-harbor/) were Texas-based Alarm Concepts, a Connecticut
company called Belpointe Sleepovation Investment, an individual in Texas named
Cedrick Williams, and Shelby Lowman, the golf pro at Trump National Golf Club
Hudson Valley.

It’s unclear if Trump knows Lowman personally. After Trump bought his Hudson
Valley golf club in 2009, the [Poughkeepsie Journal
reported](https://www.poughkeepsiejournal.com/story/news/2016/11/09/archive-
donald-trump-breathes-new-life-into-dutchess-golf-course/93570834/?gnt-
cfr=1&gca-cat=p&gca-uir=true&gca-epti=z115401e005610v115401d--54--b--54--&gca-
ft=144&gca-ds=sophi) that he visited nearly every month to oversee
renovations. Lowman was already working there as a golf pro and has remained
at the club for the past 17 years, according to his LinkedIn profile.

In addition to his work as a golf pro, Lowman paints pastoral scenes of
Trump’s golf properties. Trump has autographed copies of Lowman’s paintings to
be given out as prizes for golf competitions at the club. The golf club has
also [posted a photo](https://www.instagram.com/p/Czt74sZusLv/) of Lowman
posing with Eric Trump, who runs the Trump Organization.

A spokesperson for the Trump Organization said it “had no involvement in or
connection to this lawsuit. To the extent any current or former employees are
involved, it is entirely in their personal capacity as individual taxpayers.”

![An Instagram post featuring a photo of President Donald Trump signing a
painting of a golf course. The caption reads: “Here the first project I did
for Trump Hudson Valley. We used two of my prints for our Men’s Member Guest
Prizes. Flight winners received a 14x18” version and the overall champions
received a larger 18x24” version that we were able to get autographed by
President Trump.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/11/IMG_1330_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg?w=752)An
Instagram post from Shelby Lowman shows Trump signing his paintings of the
golf course, which were being given away as prizes for competitions at the
club. @shelbypga_golf_art via Instagram

At first, the Justice Department sought to [dismiss the Safe Harbor __
case](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28922515-irs-motion-to-dismiss-
safe-harbor/). A DOJ trial attorney argued, among other things, that the U.S.
government was not the proper target for a lawsuit about the conduct of a
government contractor. The judge rejected the motion and cleared the way for
discovery and potentially a trial.

The plaintiffs in Safe Harbor __ alleged two unauthorized disclosures of their
tax information, which would entitle them to $2,000 each under the statute. To
get more, they would have to prove actual damages. But before the case reached
the fact-finding stage, the DOJ stopped fighting the case and in August made a
[unilateral proposal](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28922516-doj-
offer-of-judgment-safe-harbor/?mode=document#document/p1/a2836215) to the five
named plaintiffs, labeled an offer of judgment, to resolve the matter by
paying them $500,000 each, court records show.

When IRS employees learned about the DOJ’s $2.5 million offer, they pointed
out that it was dramatically higher than what the law called for and was not
supported by any evidence, according to people familiar with the case and
documents seen by ProPublica.

What made the government’s offer even more unusual was who made it. The career
DOJ trial attorney working the case did not sign the proposed payout, as is
typical.

Instead, two Trump [political appointees delivered the
offer](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28922516-doj-offer-of-judgment-
safe-harbor/?mode=document#document/p2/a2836216): Brett Shumate, the head of
the DOJ’s civil division, and Joshua Wu, the deputy assistant attorney general
for the department’s tax litigation branch. (Shumate left the DOJ in early
November. He did not respond to requests for comment.)

In the past, the IRS has fought such claims. In 2022, billionaire investor Ken
Griffin [brought a similar suit](https://www.propublica.org/article/ken-
griffin-citadel-irs-propublica-lawsuit-taxes) against the agency, [dropping it
a year and a half later](https://tax.thomsonreuters.com/news/irs-issues-
apology-to-billionaire-other-tax-leak-victims/) after he received an apology
from the IRS and a pledge to improve the agency’s data security. [Griffin
received no money](https://www.politico.com/news/2024/06/25/ken-griffin-drops-
irs-leak-suit-00164870) as part of the settlement.

Lowman, Williams and Alarm Concepts did not respond to requests for comment.
Reached by phone, Linda Nussbaum, a lawyer for Belpointe, told ProPublica that
it was “news to me” that the other plaintiffs in the lawsuit had “ties to the
Trump administration.” She declined to comment further on the case.

The post [The Trump DOJ Quietly Intervened to Ink a Huge Payout to a Trump
Golf Pro](https://www.propublica.org/article/irs-settlement-golf-pro-shelby-
lowman) appeared first on [ProPublica](https://www.propublica.org).
